title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
summary: Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without s everywhere, ` ` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0]) Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent +JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge. 200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1] I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU. We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.) People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided. Try it out: DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler! title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
summary: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings. Here's a quick demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BFfbXAwRq98 Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman. I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy. To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp). I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use. title: Show HN: RealtimeVAD – trading false positives for 110ms earlier end-of-speech
summary: Hey guys. I recently watched the latency reports for my local voice assistant, which show a waveform plus silero probability for voice activity. I noticed silero lags visibly on the speech off signal. There had to be a method to get this signal closer to what I felt is optimal. My idea was to use a 10 ms energy detector with a threshold that adapts to environment or room noise. Which worked amazingly well. It created more false positives but in my speculative generation pipeline that would not matter. If it's wrong and the user continues speaking I can abort the pipeline fast. I benchmarked my solution over ~3200 turns from my assistant logs and it came out ~110 ms faster initially. Still 100 ms now after some a fix which was needed for quiet speech. I made it public if you want to have a look. If you measure it on your data I really appreciate any feedback. There's a benchmark script in the repo. Thx for reading, have a good day folks. title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force
summary: Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic ( https://axonnic.com ). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots. Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly. The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors. When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks . We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies. Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension. Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings. So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG. If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks! https://axonnic.com Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50522776 Points: 43 # Comments: 20
